en: The Questions of King Milinda:
The Introduction to the Chapter on the Puzzling Questions;
The Section on the Qualities of a Lay Follower.
5. The Qualities of a Teacher “Venerable Nāgasena, this spot of ground is free from the eight defects of counsel; and I am the supreme companion for counsel in the world.
I shall guard the secret as long as I live, and by me—[the eight qualities]...”
For these reasons, my intellect has reached a state of transformation: a pupil such as I am is difficult to find nowadays.
Toward a pupil who is practicing rightly, a teacher should conduct himself properly with those twenty-five qualities of a teacher.
What are the twenty-five qualities?
"Here, venerable Nāgasena, a teacher must constantly and continuously provide protection for his pupil;
he must know when the pupil is associating and when he is not; he must know whether he is negligent or diligent; he must know the state of his bed; he must know his illness;
he must know what food has been obtained and what has not; he must know his progress; and he must share with him whatever is in his alms-bowl."
He should be comforted with the words, “Do not fear; your purpose is being fulfilled. He should understand the person’s way of associating:
he must recognize their association in the village, their association in the monastery, and their association in the dwelling.
He should not engage in laughter or play with them, but should converse with them. Seeing a lapse, he should endure it; he should be one who acts with thorough care.
One should be one who acts without breaking [the precepts], one who acts according to what is worthy, and one who acts without remainder;
one should establish the mind of a progenitor, thinking, "May I produce this person in the crafts";
one should establish the mind of growth, thinking, "How may this person not decline?"; and one should establish the mind, thinking, "I make this person strong by the power of training."
"A mind of loving-kindness should be established; one should not abandon [the pupil] in times of misfortune; one should not be negligent regarding what ought to be done;
and when he has erred, he should be corrected in accordance with the Dhamma.
These, venerable sir, are the twenty-five qualities of a teacher. Practice rightly toward me with these qualities."
“Venerable sir, a doubt has arisen in me. There are the ‘Questions of Meṇḍaka’ spoken by the Conqueror;
in future times, disputes will arise concerning them. In future times, those as wise as you will be rare.
Grant me insight into these questions for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others.”
